title: Pre-carriage to the terminal
sceneDesc: A landscape between the shipper and the export terminal: a road, possibly a bridge, a river with barges and a railway. The chosen transport carries the container to the terminal.

narration.2: [[pre-carriage|Pre-carriage]] to {polTerminal}. Who moves me was fixed at booking: [[merchant-haulage]] or [[carrier-haulage]]. Open the choice to compare.
narration.3: Haulage mode drives liability, invoicing and who manages appointments and waiting time. Under carrier haulage the B/L can show an inland place of receipt. [TO VERIFY:v43]

caption.2: Under {incoterm}, pre-carriage is for the account of {preBy}, whatever the haulage mode.

1.many: Full, sealed and weighed, I'm leaving. How do I get to the port? Pick a transport mode.
1.*: Full, sealed and weighed, I'm leaving for the port — by truck, the usual way to reach {polTerminal}.

2.many: Mode choice depends on distance, volumes, infrastructure and cut-offs. Compare the options available to reach {polTerminal}. [TO VERIFY:v39]
2.*: {polTerminal} is reached by road: trucking is the standard pre-carriage here. [TO VERIFY:v39]

narration.3: Intermodal legs close earlier than the CY cut-off and add handlings; trucking is exposed to congestion and road weight limits. [TO VERIFY:v40]

2.reefer: Reefers travel with a [[genset]] on the road. [TO VERIFY:v57]
2.tank: DG on the road follows national rules (e.g. ADR in Europe). [TO VERIFY:v59]
2.oog: Oversize loads may need a road permit or escort. [TO VERIFY:v58]
2.*: Intermodal legs usually close earlier than the port cut-off. [TO VERIFY:v40]

1.barge: All aboard! A barge carries dozens of containers to {polTerminal}. Slower than a truck, but cheaper per box.
1.rail: I ride a train towards the port, then a short truck trip reaches the terminal.
1.*: On the road! The driver carries my booking number so the terminal knows who I am.

2.barge: Barge from an inland barge terminal to {polTerminal}: economies of scale, an extra handling and an earlier cut-off. [TO VERIFY:v40]
2.rail: Rail to a rail terminal, then a last-mile leg: two extra handlings, each with cost and time.
2.*: Road haulage. Road weight limits apply to the whole truck, so a box within its own rating can still be overweight on the road. [TO VERIFY:v13]

narration.3: In transit: the haulier carries booking and container references; ETA to the terminal is monitored against the CY cut-off ({cyCutoff}).

caption.2: Port (CY) cut-off: {cyCutoff} (illustrative). Missed = not on the load list.

narration.1: Here's the terminal. The gate is expecting me: my arrival was announced in advance. But is my paperwork ready?
narration.2: At the terminal approach: [[pre-advice]] sent and, where required, a truck appointment booked. Open the transport order to see what the gate checks. [TO VERIFY:v44]
narration.3: Pre-advice (EDI COPARN or portal) and appointment slot must match the truck, the box and the booking — otherwise the gate rejects or holds it. [TO VERIFY:v44]

3.SHA-LEH: Fog closes the Donghai Bridge for hours. The driver now expects to reach Yangshan four hours after the CY cut-off.
3.HCM-SIN-LEH: Severe congestion around Cat Lai: the driver now expects to reach the gate four hours after the CY cut-off.
3.*: A road blockade on the way to Posorja: the driver now expects to reach the gate four hours after the CY cut-off.

SHA-LEH.1: Shanghai is the world's busiest container port: around 50 million TEU a year. [TO VERIFY:v42]
SHA-LEH.2: The Donghai Bridge linking Yangshan to the mainland is about 32.5 km long — every truck delivering to Yangshan crosses it. [TO VERIFY:v41]

HCM-SIN-LEH.1: Around Ho Chi Minh City, many containers travel by river barge on the Mekong delta waterways. [TO VERIFY:v54]
HCM-SIN-LEH.2: Cat Lai is a river terminal: big ships can't reach it, which is why boxes go by feeder to a hub like Singapore — or to deep-water Cai Mep. [TO VERIFY:v54]

*.1: Ecuador is the world's largest banana exporter. [TO VERIFY:v55]
*.2: Posorja is a deep-water port built on the coast, so large ships no longer need to sail up the Guayas river to Guayaquil. [TO VERIFY:v55]

body.1: Whoever moves me, I must reach the terminal before the port deadline ({cyCutoff}, illustrative) — the [[cut-off]]. Late = I miss my ship.
body.2: CY cut-off {cyCutoff} (illustrative). Barge and rail legs have earlier cut-offs. [TO VERIFY:v40]

body.1: {polTerminal}: the port facility where I'll wait for my ship.
body.2: Receives full boxes up to the CY cut-off, stacks them for loading and reports arrivals to customs. [TO VERIFY:v45]

body.1: The island terminal is linked to the mainland by a sea bridge more than 30 km long. [TO VERIFY:v41]
body.2: Donghai Bridge (about 32.5 km). Congestion or bad weather on the bridge directly threatens cut-offs. [TO VERIFY:v41]

body.1: Roads have weight limits for the whole truck. A heavy container can be legal for the ship but too heavy for the road.
body.2: Gross vehicle weight limits are national (China: GB 1589; France: 44 t for 5+ axles). Overweight → fines, truck stopped. [TO VERIFY:v13]

body.1: On the road, a diesel generator keeps my cooling unit running.
body.2: Clip-on or underslung [[genset]] keeps the reefer powered between plug points; fuel and function checked before departure. [TO VERIFY:v57]

body.1: A message telling the terminal I'm coming: booking number, container number, ship. Without it, the gate may turn me away.

points.1: Container, seal and booking must match the terminal's pre-advice exactly; a single digit wrong = gate rejection or hold. [TO VERIFY:v44]
points.2: The CY cut-off is the latest arrival time. Some terminals also require a truck appointment slot. [TO VERIFY:v44]
points.3: Special cargo has extra road rules: genset for reefers, DG documents and placards, permits for oversize loads. [TO VERIFY:v57] [TO VERIFY:v58] [TO VERIFY:v59]

2.prompt: What does the terminal gate match the truck against?

options.text: The pre-advice / booking data: booking number, container number, seal (and appointment where required)

options.fb: Invoices are for customs and the buyer, not the gate.
The B/L doesn't exist yet for this box, and never travels with the truck.
The driver is checked, but the box must match an expected delivery.

2.explain: Terminals accept full export boxes only when they match a pre-advised booking; mismatches mean refusal or hold. [TO VERIFY:v44]

3.prompt: The pre-advice shows a container number with a wrong check digit. The truck is at the gate. Most likely outcome?

options.text: Gate rejection or hold until the forwarder corrects the pre-advice; the truck waits or is turned away
The gate clerk corrects the digit on the spot and lets the box in
options.fb: Some terminals allow manual correction, but data ownership stays with the sender; the default is hold.

options.text: The box enters; the B/L will be corrected later
options.fb: Entering under wrong data breaks traceability to the booking and load list.
A data mismatch is an operational issue, not a customs offence.

3.explain: Check digits exist to catch typos (ISO 6346). Clean data avoids waiting time and cut-off risk. [TO VERIFY:v32] [TO VERIFY:v44]

documents: **Transport / haulage order** — merchant → haulier, or carrier → subcontractor.
**Pre-advice** (e.g. EDI COPARN) and truck appointment. [TO VERIFY:v44]
**VGM** already transmitted — some terminals check it at gate-in. [TO VERIFY:v01]
**Barge or rail consignment note** for intermodal legs.
costs: **Pre-carriage** — carrier haulage tariff or the merchant's own contract.
**Waiting time** beyond free loading time. [TO VERIFY:v12]
**Intermodal handling** at barge or rail terminals. [TO VERIFY:v40]
risks: **Arrival after the CY cut-off** → shut out, rolled (+7 days on a weekly service).
**Pre-advice mismatch** → refused at the gate, waiting time.

risks.text: **Genset failure** on a reefer → temperature excursion before the terminal. [TO VERIFY:v57]

jobs: **Inland / intermodal operations** — haulier, barge and rail planning.
**Customer service** — cut-off monitoring and rollover communication.
**D&D / finance** — waiting time and detention invoicing.

incoNote.EXW: Under EXW, the buyer organises and pays this trip — risk passed at the seller's door.
incoNote.FCA: Under FCA (terminal), risk and cost pass when this truck arrives at the terminal, ready for unloading.
incoNote.FAS: Under FAS, risk passes when the goods are 'alongside' — for containers, effectively at the terminal.
incoNote.CPT: Under CPT, risk passes when the box is handed to the carrier at the terminal; the seller still pays carriage to destination.
incoNote.CIP: Under CIP, risk passes when the box is handed to the carrier at the terminal; the seller still pays carriage and insurance.
incoNote.*: The seller pays this trip and still carries the risk.

1: Pre-carriage brings the full container from the shipper to the export terminal, usually by truck.
It must arrive before the port deadline (cut-off).
The terminal must be expecting it: that's the pre-advice.
2: Merchant vs carrier haulage changes who contracts, who invoices and where the carrier's responsibility starts.
Mode choice (truck, barge, rail) drives cost, emissions and cut-off timing.
Pre-advice and appointments are hard constraints; late = shut-out.
3: Ask for a cut-off extension before the cut-off, not after — and document the answer.
Data quality (check digits, seal numbers) prevents gate holds.
Special cargo adds road rules: genset, DG regulations, oversize permits.

1.prompt: I'm almost at the terminal. Is my paperwork ready? What happens next?
1.hint: Before a container can leave a country, two organisations need information about it: the carrier and customs.

options.text: In parallel, the paperwork is finished: shipping instructions to the carrier and an export customs declaration.
options.confirm: Yes! A container travels twice: physically, and as data. The carrier needs the shipping instructions for the Bill of Lading, and customs must approve the export. Under {incoterm}, export customs is handled by the {exportBy}.

options.text: The terminal loads me straight onto the ship as soon as I arrive.
options.why: The ship may not even be in port yet; the terminal first checks me in, stores me and plans where I go on board.
options.realLife: Containers usually wait a few days in the terminal yard. Without customs approval, the terminal won't load me.
options.whenRight: Some special cargo goes directly to the ship's side, by prior agreement.

options.text: Customs opens and checks every container before it enters the port.
options.why: Customs check data first and select only a small share for physical inspection, based on risk.
options.realLife: If I'm selected, I'm moved to an inspection area: extra cost and delay — but it's the exception.
options.whenRight: When customs selects a container after its risk check.

2.prompt: Your {mode} delivery is approaching {polTerminal} before the port cut-off; VGM already transmitted. What happens next?

options.text: The data flow closes in parallel: SI before the SI cut-off, export declaration by the exporter's broker, and the carrier's advance cargo declarations.
options.confirm: Correct. Physical and documentary flows run in parallel, each with its own cut-off. Under {incoterm}, export clearance is the {exportBy}'s job. [TO VERIFY:v45]

options.text: The carrier lodges the export declaration as part of the ocean freight, using the booking data.
options.why: The exporter (or its broker) is the declarant; booking data lacks HS codes, values and invoice details.
options.realLife: No declaration = no customs release = not loaded.
options.whenRight: Some carriers sell brokerage as a separate service, under the exporter's mandate.

options.text: No more data is needed: the draft B/L is generated from the booking confirmation.
options.why: The booking has no consignee, final cargo description, package count or seal. The B/L is built from the SI.
options.realLife: Late or missing SI → late-SI fee, B/L on hold, shut-out risk. [TO VERIFY:v12]
options.whenRight: Portals can pre-fill the SI with booking data — the shipper still completes it.

options.text: Customs physically inspects the box at the gate; the terminal only receives inspected containers.
options.why: Customs controls are risk-based: most boxes are released electronically.
options.realLife: If selected, the box moves to an inspection area: costs and delay for the cargo side.
options.whenRight: When targeted after risk analysis, or for controlled goods. [TO VERIFY:v19]

3.prompt: Case: the truck will reach the gate four hours after the CY cut-off. What is the best course of action?

options.text: Before the cut-off, ask the carrier's export desk for a late-gate approval with the new ETA; if refused, rebook on the next sailing and inform the customer at once.
options.confirm: Right. Late-gate acceptance depends on the terminal's load planning and is easier before the plan is closed; it may carry a fee. Either way, the customer hears it from you first. [TO VERIFY:v12] [TO VERIFY:v31]

options.text: Let the truck arrive and hope the gate accepts it.
options.why: After the cut-off the box isn't on the load list; the gate may refuse or accept it only for the next vessel.
options.realLife: Storage starts, the box waits a week, and the customer finds out last.

options.text: Ask the terminal to delay the vessel's departure.
options.why: Vessels run on fixed berth windows serving many customers.
options.realLife: Not possible for one box; ships only wait for major operational reasons.
options.whenRight: Never for a single late container.

options.text: Send the box to a different terminal with a later cut-off.
options.why: The box is booked on a specific vessel at a specific terminal.
options.realLife: A box at the wrong terminal must be shifted: cost and almost certain shut-out.
options.whenRight: Only if the carrier rebooks it on a service calling that terminal.
